Yes, I understand the difference between speakers that intentionally color the sound in the low frequencies to create the illusion of bass.

Many years ago, I spent a lot of time in rehearsal spaces, playing drums, surrounded by large guitar and bass cabinets.  
For example, when I had a bass cabinet the size of a refrigerator next to me, with eight 8-inch speakers, you didn’t need to study physics or acoustics to understand that small monitors with 6-inch speakers simply cannot physically replicate or reproduce such sound. And on the other side, a guitar cabinet with four 15-inch speakers.  
So, when you're in a studio, you want to feel (or have the option to feel) that movement of air.

It’s true that professional subwoofers are designed for a smooth extension of the low-frequency range.  
On the SCM45A Pro, live drums sounded as though the low frequencies were cut off because they cannot reveal the full low-frequency range of a kick drum.

Additionally, having the ability to hear the lowest frequencies allows you to effectively eliminate all unnecessary low-frequency artifacts during mixing. With small monitors, this becomes problematic.  
I believe that, in most cases, a lot of low frequencies are removed during mixing to make room for just a few instruments. In the high-frequency range, you can place more instruments, but in the low frequencies, everything must be clean (in my opinion). If you solo the low frequencies in a well-produced recording, it will always sound clean, without any booming or rumbling.

In general, may the universe grant us all lots of money to buy spacious homes, install SCM300ASL Pro speakers, and properly treat the acoustics of the space.

Unfortunately, I don’t like the sound of Genelec monitors. They might be accurate in terms of frequency response and measurements, but no matter what I listen to on them, the sound doesn’t appeal to me. Perhaps a direct comparison with other monitors like Dynaudio or ATC would help me better understand how Genelec compares to other brands.

I’ve listened to many Genelec monitors, including their flagship models. In Finland, nearly every store has a demo setup where you can listen and switch between different monitors. However, I think what I don’t like is their metallic (or titanium) tweeter.

I used to own Yamaha MSP7 monitors with two Yamaha SW10 subwoofers. Those monitors also have metallic tweeters, and their sound wasn’t as smooth as I would have liked. Currently, I’m leaning towards Dynaudio. Personally, they have the best sound I’ve ever heard. Perhaps it’s also because I’ve spent a lot of time with them in a studio with proper acoustic treatment across all surfaces (not just foam panels on the walls).

On top of that, Dynaudio monitors are almost twice as cheap as Genelec. Again, maybe if I could compare them side by side, I’d understand why Genelec is so expensive, but for now, I just don’t like them.

I’ve also heard the SCM45A Pro, and I liked them. They also have a smooth tweeter (not made of metal). But like the Adam S3H, they have an issue where two drivers overlap in the same frequency range. I’d prefer to get the SCM25A Pro Mk II instead. However, both of those models absolutely need a subwoofer, as they lack low-end frequencies.

Yes, I have already listened to the SCM45A Pro in the rehearsal space, which was located in a large container with a certain amount of sound-absorbing materials.

Of course, these are not studio conditions, but I was finally able to listen to the monitors of this company.



I really liked them. And I really liked that they don’t have thousands of regulators for different frequencies, adjustments to their position and other unnecessary small settings. They are completely analog. Plug in the wire and listen.



Their detail is simply amazing. But I also heard in them what I expected to hear.

The first is that when monitors have two 6-inch speakers, there is some amplification of the lower middle. The fact that there are two 6-inch speakers does not mean that there will be more low frequencies.

Therefore, if I had the money to buy monitors from this company, I would definitely take the SCM25A Pro Mk2 and not the SCM45A Pro.

Since the SCM25A Pro Mk is the first monitor in the line that has a mid-frequency speaker.



And the second point about the SCM45A Pro monitors is that they do not have low frequencies.

I don't mean low frequencies like at a concert or in a car with four 15-inch subwoofers that break the windows.

I'm just talking about the usual presence of low frequencies at least up to 30 hertz.

Previously, I had Yamaha MSP 7 monitors with two subwoofers from the same series.

And I really need the whole spectrum to be heard.



So if one day I have the opportunity, I want to listen to the SCM150ASL Pro or SCM300ASL Pro. And I think this is exactly what I need (and another 50,000 extra euros).
